::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
This note follows [Forward Propagation & Activation Functions](../forward-propagation/index.qmd)
in the [Neural Networks](../index.qmd) module. Forward propagation computes a
network's output; **backpropagation** computes how the loss changes with every
weight, so that gradient descent can train the network.

🧪 The figures here come from a companion [NumPy notebook](demo.ipynb), which
implements the derivation, checks it against finite differences, and trains the
network.

📄 Prefer the raw version? See my [original notes](source.qmd), a verbatim
transcription of the handwritten pages, mistakes and all.
:::

## The network and notation

The example network has 4 inputs, two hidden layers with 5 and 3 nodes, and 2
outputs. Layers are numbered $0$ (input) to $3$ (output), and a bracketed
superscript says which layer a quantity belongs to:

- $x^{[0]}$ is the input, and $x^{[l]}$ is layer $l$'s output vector;
- $W^{[l]}$ holds the weights from layer $l-1$ into layer $l$, with
  $w^{[l]}_{ij}$ on the edge **into** node $i$ **from** node $j$ (destination
  first, as in the forward-propagation note);
- $a^{[l]} = W^{[l]} x^{[l-1]}$ is layer $l$'s pre-activation, and
  $x^{[l]} = f^{[l]}(a^{[l]})$ its output, where $f^{[l]}$ is that layer's
  activation function.

In the figure each split node holds $a$ on the left and $x$ on the right.

{{< embed demo.ipynb#fig-network >}}

| Matrix | Shape | Vector | Length |
|---|---|---|---|
| $W^{[1]}$ | $5 \times 4$ | $x^{[0]}$ | 4 |
| $W^{[2]}$ | $3 \times 5$ | $a^{[1]}, x^{[1]}$ | 5 |
| $W^{[3]}$ | $2 \times 3$ | $a^{[2]}, x^{[2]}$ | 3 |
| | | $a^{[3]}, x^{[3]}$ | 2 |

As in my notes, there are no biases; I come back to them at the end.

## Forward pass as a nested function

Substituting each layer into the next writes the whole network as one nested
function of the input:

$$
x^{[3]} = f^{[3]}\big(a^{[3]}\big)
= f^{[3]}\big(W^{[3]} x^{[2]}\big)
= \cdots
= f^{[3]}\Big(W^{[3]} f^{[2]}\big(W^{[2]} f^{[1]}(W^{[1]} x^{[0]})\big)\Big).
$$

Backpropagation is the chain rule applied to this nesting, peeling it from the
outside in. $W^{[3]}$ sits in the outermost layer, so its gradient is the easiest
to compute; $W^{[1]}$ is buried deepest.

## The loss

For a single data point with input $x^{[0]}$ and ground truth $t$, the error is
$e = t - x^{[3]}$ and the loss is half the squared error:

$$
L = \tfrac12 e^T e = \tfrac12 \Big( \big(t_1 - x^{[3]}_1\big)^2 + \big(t_2 - x^{[3]}_2\big)^2 \Big).
$$

The goal is $\partial L / \partial W^{[l]}$ for each layer: a matrix the same
shape as $W^{[l]}$, whose entry $(i, j)$ is $\partial L / \partial w^{[l]}_{ij}$.

## The output layer, one weight at a time

Take one output-layer weight $w^{[3]}_{ij}$. Differentiating the loss gives one
term per output:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{[3]}_{ij}}
= \big(t_1 - x^{[3]}_1\big) \frac{\partial \big(t_1 - x^{[3]}_1\big)}{\partial w^{[3]}_{ij}}
+ \big(t_2 - x^{[3]}_2\big) \frac{\partial \big(t_2 - x^{[3]}_2\big)}{\partial w^{[3]}_{ij}}.
$$

Two observations collapse this:

1. **Only output $i$ depends on $w^{[3]}_{ij}$.** The weight sits on an edge into
   node $i$, so the other output's term is zero. (For $w^{[3]}_{11}$, the term
   for output 2 is $(t_2 - x^{[3]}_2) \cdot 0$.)
2. **Only one term of $a^{[3]}_i$ depends on it.** In
   $a^{[3]}_i = w^{[3]}_{i1} x^{[2]}_1 + w^{[3]}_{i2} x^{[2]}_2 + w^{[3]}_{i3} x^{[2]}_3$,
   the derivative with respect to $w^{[3]}_{ij}$ is $x^{[2]}_j$.

Applying the chain rule through $x^{[3]}_i = f^{[3]}(a^{[3]}_i)$:

$$
\boxed{\;
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{[3]}_{ij}} = -\big(t_i - x^{[3]}_i\big)\, f'^{[3]}\big(a^{[3]}_i\big)\, x^{[2]}_j
\;}
$$

Read it as three factors: how wrong output $i$ is, how sensitive output $i$ is to
its pre-activation, and how large the input along this edge is.

## The output layer as a matrix

Writing all six entries out, every row shares the factor
$-(t_i - x^{[3]}_i) f'^{[3]}(a^{[3]}_i)$ and every column shares $x^{[2]}_j$. So
the gradient matrix is a column vector times a row vector, an **outer product**:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{[3]}}
= \underbrace{-\big(t - x^{[3]}\big) \odot f'^{[3]}\big(a^{[3]}\big)}_{2 \times 1}\;
\underbrace{\big(x^{[2]}\big)^T}_{1 \times 3},
$$

where $\odot$ is element-wise multiplication. The first factor is important
enough to get a name:

$$
\delta^{[3]} = -\big(t - x^{[3]}\big) \odot f'^{[3]}\big(a^{[3]}\big),
\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{[3]}} = \delta^{[3]} \big(x^{[2]}\big)^T.
$$

::: {.callout-note title="My note: what the delta means" icon=false}
Comparing with the boxed formula, $\delta^{[3]}_i = \partial L / \partial a^{[3]}_i$:
the delta is the gradient of the loss with respect to a layer's
**pre-activation**. That's the quantity that gets passed backward. Every weight
gradient is then "delta of the node the edge goes into" times "output of the node
it comes from".
:::

{{< embed demo.ipynb#fig-outer-product >}}

## The hidden layers: the delta recursion

My notes state the result for the hidden layers directly ("use the chain rule").
Each layer's delta comes from the next layer's:

$$
\delta^{[2]} = \big(W^{[3]}\big)^T \delta^{[3]} \odot f'^{[2]}\big(a^{[2]}\big),
\qquad
\delta^{[1]} = \big(W^{[2]}\big)^T \delta^{[2]} \odot f'^{[1]}\big(a^{[1]}\big),
$$

and the gradients keep the same outer-product form:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{[2]}} = \delta^{[2]} \big(x^{[1]}\big)^T,
\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{[1]}} = \delta^{[1]} \big(x^{[0]}\big)^T.
$$

::: {.callout-note title="My note: deriving $\delta^{[2]}$" icon=false}
Hidden node $j$ in layer 2 affects the loss through **every** output, because its
output $x^{[2]}_j$ feeds both $a^{[3]}_1$ and $a^{[3]}_2$. The chain rule sums
over those paths:

$$
\delta^{[2]}_j = \frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{[2]}_j}
= \sum_{i} \underbrace{\frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{[3]}_i}}_{\delta^{[3]}_i}\,
\underbrace{\frac{\partial a^{[3]}_i}{\partial x^{[2]}_j}}_{w^{[3]}_{ij}}\,
\underbrace{\frac{\partial x^{[2]}_j}{\partial a^{[2]}_j}}_{f'^{[2]}(a^{[2]}_j)}
= \Big( \sum_i w^{[3]}_{ij}\, \delta^{[3]}_i \Big) f'^{[2]}\big(a^{[2]}_j\big).
$$

The sum runs down **column** $j$ of $W^{[3]}$, which is row $j$ of
$(W^{[3]})^T$, giving the matrix form above. The forward pass sends signals along
the edges with $W$; the backward pass sends deltas along the same edges in
reverse with $W^T$. Then $\partial L / \partial w^{[2]}_{jk} = \delta^{[2]}_j\, x^{[1]}_k$,
exactly as for the output layer, and the same step gives $\delta^{[1]}$.
:::

## The algorithm

::: {.callout-important title="Backpropagation (one data point)" icon=false}
1. **Forward:** for $l = 1, 2, 3$, compute $a^{[l]} = W^{[l]} x^{[l-1]}$ and
   $x^{[l]} = f^{[l]}(a^{[l]})$. Keep them all.
2. **Output delta:** $\delta^{[3]} = -\big(t - x^{[3]}\big) \odot f'^{[3]}\big(a^{[3]}\big)$.
3. **Backward:** for $l = 2, 1$, compute
   $\delta^{[l]} = \big(W^{[l+1]}\big)^T \delta^{[l+1]} \odot f'^{[l]}\big(a^{[l]}\big)$.
4. **Gradients:** $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial W^{[l]}} = \delta^{[l]} \big(x^{[l-1]}\big)^T$ for every layer.
:::

The backward pass costs about as much as the forward pass, because it is the same
matrix–vector products run in reverse. The notebook confirms the formulas by
comparing them with finite differences, which nudge each weight by $\pm\varepsilon$
and need two forward passes **per weight**. They agree to about $10^{-10}$:

{{< embed demo.ipynb#fig-gradcheck >}}

## Training

With the gradients in hand, gradient descent updates every weight matrix in the
direction that lowers the loss, with learning rate $\eta$:

$$
W^{[l]}_\text{new} = W^{[l]} - \eta\, \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{[l]}}.
$$

Repeating forward pass, backward pass, and update on the single data point drives
the outputs to the target:

{{< embed demo.ipynb#fig-train-single >}}

For a dataset of $N$ points, the loss is the sum of the per-point losses, so its
gradient is the sum of the per-point gradients. The algorithm doesn't change; you
run it on each point (or on all of them at once, stacked as matrix columns) and
add up the results.

::: {.callout-note title="What my notes leave out: the bias" icon=false}
Real layers compute $a^{[l]} = W^{[l]} x^{[l-1]} + b^{[l]}$. Since
$\partial a^{[l]}_i / \partial b^{[l]}_i = 1$, the bias gradient is just the
delta, $\partial L / \partial b^{[l]} = \delta^{[l]}$, and the rest of the
algorithm is unchanged.

Without biases, the notebook found something I didn't expect. With odd
activations like $\tanh$, a bias-free network computes an odd function: it maps
$-x$ to the opposite of what it maps $x$ to. It then **cannot** learn a rule that
gives $x$ and $-x$ the same label, such as "$x_1$ and $x_4$ have the same sign",
and stays at chance however long it trains. Adding biases fixes it:

{{< embed demo.ipynb#fig-train-batch >}}
:::

## Clarifications on my handwritten notes

- **"$f^{[3]}$ is identity" (struck out).** I started by assuming a linear
  output layer and then kept $f^{[3]}$ general. With an identity output,
  $f'^{[3]} = 1$ and the output delta is just $\delta^{[3]} = -(t - x^{[3]}) = -e$.
- **Overwritten indices on page 3.** In the first line I overwrote the weights in
  output 1's term to read $w_{i1}, w_{i2}, w_{i3}$; they should stay
  $w_{11}, w_{12}, w_{13}$ there. The next line, which keeps only output $i$'s
  term, is right.
- **The row vector on page 3** ends with $x^{[3]}_3$; it should be $x^{[2]}_3$, as
  in $(x^{[2]})^T$ on the next line.
- **Order of operations in the recursion.**
  $\big(W^{[l+1]}\big)^T \delta^{[l+1]} \odot f'^{[l]}(a^{[l]})$ means: do the
  matrix–vector product first, then multiply element-wise.
